title: Loops
summary: Repeat work automatically — walk through collections with for loops and keep going until a condition changes with while loops.
objectives: Use a for loop to walk through every item in a collection
Generate sequences of numbers with range()
Use a while loop to repeat until a condition becomes false
Control loops with break and continue
Avoid infinite loops by always changing the condition
Build up results by looping with an accumulator variable

quiz.q: Which loop should you use when you know the collection you want to walk through?
quiz.why: A for loop is built for iterating over a known collection or sequence, visiting each item once.
range(start, stop) includes start but stops BEFORE stop, so you get 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7.

quiz.q: What is the difference between break and continue?
quiz.answer: break exits the loop entirely; continue skips the rest of the current iteration and moves to the next one.
quiz.why: break stops looping altogether, while continue only abandons the current pass and carries on with the next item.

quiz.q: What usually causes an infinite loop in a while loop?
options: Forgetting to change the condition variable
quiz.why: If the condition never becomes false because nothing inside the loop updates it, the loop runs forever.

quiz.q: True or false — a for loop in Python can iterate directly over the characters of a string.
quiz.why: True. Strings are sequences, so 'for ch in word' visits each character one at a time.

quiz.q: What is an accumulator in a loop?
quiz.answer: A variable defined before the loop that you build up (add to or append to) on each pass to collect a running result.
quiz.why: For example, total = 0 before the loop, then total = total + n inside it sums every value.

body_markdown:
## Why loops?

Computers are brilliant at doing the same thing over and over without getting bored. A **loop** is how you tell Python to repeat a block of code. Without loops you would copy and paste the same lines once per item — unthinkable when you have a thousand items.

As a maths graduate, think of it like a summation sign. *Σ from i=1 to n* says "do this for every i". A loop is that idea made executable.

## The for loop

A **for loop** walks through every item in a collection — a list, a string, a range — and runs its body once per item. The indented block is the body.

```python
names = ["Dami", "Ada", "Sam"]
for name in names:
    print("Hello, " + name)
```

Each time round, `name` holds the next item. The loop ends automatically when the collection is exhausted.

## Counting with range()

When you want numbers rather than an existing list, use `range`. Note that `range(start, stop)` **stops before** `stop`.

```python
for i in range(1, 6):
    print(i)        # prints 1 2 3 4 5
```

A classic use is an **accumulator** — a variable you build up on each pass.

```python
total = 0
for n in range(1, 101):
    total = total + n
print(total)        # 5050
```

## The while loop

A **while loop** repeats *as long as* a condition stays true. Use it when you don't know in advance how many times to loop.

```python
count = 5
while count > 0:
    print(count)
    count = count - 1   # MUST change the condition
print("Lift off!")
```

The golden rule: something inside the loop must eventually make the condition false, or you get an **infinite loop**.

## break and continue

`break` exits the loop immediately. `continue` skips the rest of the current pass and jumps to the next item.

```python
for n in range(1, 10):
    if n == 5:
        break       # stop completely at 5
    if n % 2 == 0:
        continue    # skip even numbers
    print(n)        # prints 1 3
```

## Your task

Write a loop that prints the **times table** for a number of your choice (e.g. 1 through 12), then add a `while` loop that keeps asking until the user types "quit".

slides.title: Loops in Python
slides.narration: Welcome back to Month One of your journey from maths graduate to A I engineer. In this lesson we tackle loops, the tool that lets your code repeat work automatically. By the end you'll be comfortable with for loops, while loops, the range function, and how to control a loop with break and continue.

slides.title: Why loops?
bullets: Loops repeat a block of code for you.
No copy-paste for every item.
Like a summation sign in maths.
Essential for processing data.
slides.narration: So why do we need loops? Computers are fantastic at doing the same thing over and over without getting tired. Instead of copying and pasting the same lines once per item, a loop runs them automatically for every item. As a maths graduate, think of the summation sign: do this for every i from one to n. A loop is exactly that idea made runnable.

slides.title: The for loop
bullets: Walks through every item in a collection.
The variable holds the next item each pass.
Ends automatically when items run out.
slides.narration: The most common loop is the for loop. It walks through every item in a collection, one at a time. Here the variable name holds Dami on the first pass, Ada on the second, and Sam on the third. The indented block runs once for each item, and the loop stops by itself when the list is exhausted.

slides.title: Counting with range()
bullets: range() generates numbers for you.
range(1, 6) gives 1, 2, 3, 4, 5.
It stops BEFORE the second number.
slides.narration: Often you want numbers rather than an existing list. That's what range is for. Be careful with the boundaries: range of one comma six gives you one, two, three, four, five. It includes the start but stops just before the stop value. This off-by-one rule catches everyone at first, so keep an eye on it.

slides.title: Building up a result
bullets: An accumulator collects a running result.
Set it before the loop starts.
Update it on every pass.
slides.code:
total = 0
for n in range(1, 101):
    total = total + n
print(total)   # 5050
slides.narration: One of the most useful patterns is the accumulator. You create a variable before the loop, here total starting at zero, and you add to it on every pass. This example sums every number from one to one hundred and prints five thousand and fifty. The same pattern works for counting, joining text, or building a list.

slides.title: The while loop
bullets: Repeats as long as a condition is true.
Use it when you don't know the count.
Something must change the condition.
slides.code:
count = 5
while count > 0:
    print(count)
    count = count - 1
print("Lift off!")
slides.narration: Sometimes you don't know in advance how many times to loop. That's where the while loop shines. It keeps running as long as its condition stays true. Here we count down from five. Notice the crucial line that subtracts one from count each pass. Without it, the condition would stay true forever.

slides.title: Avoiding infinite loops
bullets: An infinite loop never stops.
Cause: the condition never becomes false.
Always update the condition variable.
Press Ctrl + C to stop a runaway loop.
slides.narration: The biggest danger with while loops is the infinite loop, where the condition never becomes false and your program runs forever. The fix is simple but vital: make sure something inside the loop moves you toward the exit. If you ever get stuck in one, press Control C in the terminal to stop it.

slides.title: break and continue
bullets: break exits the loop completely.
continue skips to the next item.
Both react to conditions inside the loop.
slides.narration: Two keywords give you fine control inside a loop. break stops the whole loop immediately, like an emergency exit. continue abandons just the current pass and jumps straight to the next item. In this example we stop completely when we reach five, and along the way we skip every even number, so it prints only one and three.

slides.title: Looping over strings
bullets: Strings are sequences too.
for visits each character in turn.
Great for counting or filtering letters.
slides.code:
for ch in "AI":
    print(ch)   # A then I
slides.narration: Here's a handy fact: a string is a sequence, so you can loop straight over its characters. This for loop prints A then I, one letter per pass. It's perfect for tasks like counting vowels, cleaning text, or checking each character, which you'll do a lot when preparing data for A I models.

slides.title: Common mistakes
bullets: Forgetting range stops one early.
Infinite while loops.
Wrong indentation in the body.
Mixing up break and continue.
slides.narration: Let's flag the traps that catch beginners. One: forgetting that range stops one short of its second number. Two: infinite while loops because nothing changes the condition. Three: wrong indentation, so lines run outside the loop by accident. And four: confusing break, which exits entirely, with continue, which only skips one pass. Spot these and you'll debug far faster.

bullets: for loops walk through collections.
range() generates numbers, stopping one early.
while loops run until a condition is false.
break exits; continue skips a pass.
Task: print a times table, then loop until quit.
slides.narration: Let's recap. The for loop walks through every item in a collection, and range generates numbers for you, stopping one short. The while loop runs as long as its condition stays true, so always change that condition. break exits the loop, while continue skips a single pass. Your task before the next lesson: write a loop that prints a times table, then wrap it in a while loop that keeps asking until the user types quit. Great work, and I'll see you in the next lesson.
